name: Huperzine A

angle.text: Huperzine A is a club-moss extract floated in height-maxxing as a way to raise growth hormone by lowering somatostatin. It is approved for Alzheimer's in China and sold as a nootropic, and no study has tested the height claim, which forum posters also dispute.

summary: Club-moss cholinesterase inhibitor sold as a nootropic and floated in height-maxxing; no height study exists.
note: Forum height claims rest on an unconfirmed somatostatin theory; clinical work is on Alzheimer's disease.
currentQuick:
Huperzine A is an alkaloid from Chinese club moss that inhibits acetylcholinesterase. It is a prescription drug for Alzheimer's disease in China and a supplement elsewhere.
On looksmax.org it is discussed for height-maxxing via a theory that it raises growth hormone. No study has tested it for height, and forum users themselves dispute the theory.
How it works: It blocks acetylcholinesterase, raising acetylcholine levels in the brain. The forum theory that it also inhibits somatostatin was not found in the studies reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Grokipedia lists mild nausea, dizziness and insomnia and possible interactions with other cholinesterase inhibitors or anticholinergic drugs. It is sold as a supplement in the US.
deepLead:
Huperzine A is a plant alkaloid isolated from the Chinese club moss Huperzia serrata and a potent, reversible inhibitor of the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, which breaks down acetylcholine . Grokipedia states that it has been approved as a prescription drug for Alzheimer's disease in China since 1996 and is sold elsewhere as a dietary supplement .
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed mainly in height-maxxing, where some guides pair it with growth-hormone secretagogues on the theory that it lowers somatostatin and so raises growth hormone . Other forum users dispute this theory, saying they found no study linking huperzine A to somatostatin inhibition or height .
No published human trial has tested huperzine A for height or any other appearance outcome. Clinical research has concentrated on Alzheimer's disease and cognition .

name: Bacopa monnieri

angle.text: Bacopa, or brahmi, is taken as a memory nootropic and for stress, with users stacking it for study. Trials are small and reviews call the cognition evidence inconclusive, and appearance effects are not studied.

summary: Ayurvedic "brahmi" herb sold as a memory nootropic; trials are small and reviews call the evidence for cognition inconclusive.
note: FDA has sent warning letters over unproven disease claims on Bacopa products; not approved as a drug.
currentQuick:
Bacopa monnieri is a creeping wetland herb used for centuries in Ayurvedic medicine, where it is called brahmi and associated with memory and learning. Today extracts are sold as dietary supplements and discussed as a nootropic.
Small human trials have looked at memory and cognition in healthy adults and older people, but Wikipedia reports no good evidence that it improves cognitive performance, and the research literature describes results that vary with extract type. It has no documented role in appearance treatment.
How it works: Its main constituents are bacosides, triterpenoid saponins. Laboratory and animal work reports antioxidant activity and effects on cholinergic and other neurotransmitter systems, but how this relates to human cognition is not established.
Risks and caveats: The most commonly reported effects are nausea, increased bowel motility and stomach upset. In 2019 the US FDA sent warning letters to supplement makers over unproven claims (Alzheimer's, anxiety, blood pressure and others) and stated that no Bacopa product is approved for medical use.
deepLead:
Bacopa monnieri, known as brahmi or water hyssop, is a creeping perennial herb of tropical and subtropical wetlands that is used in Ayurvedic medicine, where it has traditionally been associated with memory and learning. Its best-characterised constituents are the bacosides, a family of dammarane-type triterpenoid saponins.
In supplement markets it is sold as a "nootropic". Reviews describe preclinical work on antioxidant and neuropharmacological effects, while Wikipedia states that there is no good evidence that it improves cognitive performance and memory. Grokipedia (an AI-generated encyclopedia) describes randomized trials as suggesting possible cognitive benefits with results varying by extract and dose.
Bacopa is not an appearance intervention; its presence in looksmaxxing-adjacent "recovery" and nootropic discussions reflects general interest in cognition and stress. In the United States it is not an approved drug, and the FDA issued warning letters in 2019 about unproven health claims.

name: Ginkgo biloba

angle.text: Ginkgo is sold for memory and circulation, and some users take it as a general nootropic. Large reviews have not found conclusive cognitive benefit, and no appearance outcome has been studied.

summary: Leaf extract of the ancient ginkgo tree sold as a memory and circulation supplement; large reviews find no conclusive benefit and it carries bleeding-interaction cautions.
note: May interact with anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs; IARC lists the extract as possibly carcinogenic (Group 2B).
currentQuick:
Ginkgo biloba extract comes from the leaves of the ginkgo tree, a "living fossil" native to China. It has long been used in traditional Chinese medicine and is now one of the best-known herbal supplements for memory and circulation.
Wikipedia reports that no high-quality evidence supports its use for memory or attention in healthy people and that the US NCCIH says it has not been conclusively proven effective for any condition. In the EU a standardised extract is registered as a herbal medicine for mild dementia. It is not an appearance treatment.
How it works: Extracts contain flavonoids and terpene lactones and have been studied for antioxidant and blood-flow related effects; the mechanisms behind any clinical effect remain unsettled.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include stomach upset, headache, dizziness and bleeding risk, and interactions with warfarin and antiplatelet drugs are a concern. Ginkgolic acids can cause allergic skin reactions and eating many raw seeds can cause ginkgotoxin poisoning. IARC classified the extract as a possible carcinogen in 2016.
deepLead:
Ginkgo biloba, the ginkgo or maidenhair tree, is a long-lived deciduous tree native to China and the only living species in its division. Standardised leaf extracts are sold as supplements and, in some European countries, as herbal medicines for cognitive complaints.
Wikipedia reports use in traditional Chinese medicine since at least the 11th century and states that there is no conclusive evidence for any of its traditional uses. The US NCCIH has said it has never been conclusively proven effective for any condition, while a 2014 European Medicines Agency committee concluded that the leaf extract is effective and safe for improving cognition and quality of life in mild dementia.
Ginkgo has no established role in appearance treatment; it appears in looksmaxxing-adjacent nootropic and "recovery" discussion as a general cognitive and circulation supplement.

name: Vinpocetine

angle.text: Vinpocetine is a prescription drug in parts of Europe and a US supplement that users take for memory and focus. Evidence in dementia or stroke is described as unsupported by full reviews, and appearance use is untested.

summary: Semi-synthetic periwinkle derivative sold in Europe as a prescription drug and in the US as a supplement; evidence for benefit in dementia or stroke is described as unsupported by full reviews, and the FDA warns about pregnancy.
note: FDA warned in 2019 that it may cause miscarriage or harm fetal development; US regulators consider it an unapproved new drug.
currentQuick:
Vinpocetine is a synthetic derivative of vincamine, an alkaloid from the lesser periwinkle. It was developed in Hungary and sold there as Cavinton, and has been used for decades in parts of Europe and Asia for cerebrovascular disorders. In the US it is sold as a "nootropic" supplement.
Wikipedia says the evidence does not fully support a benefit in either dementia or stroke. There are no studies of vinpocetine for appearance.
How it works: Proposed actions include sodium channel blockade, reduced calcium influx, antioxidant activity, PDE1 inhibition and inhibition of IKK, which affects NF-kappaB inflammatory signalling.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include flushing, nausea, dizziness, dry mouth, headache, heartburn and blood-pressure changes. The FDA warned in 2019 that it may cause miscarriage or harm fetal development. US regulators regard it as an unapproved new drug and a 2015 analysis found many supplement labels inaccurate.
deepLead:
Vinpocetine (ethyl apovincaminate) is a synthetic derivative of the vinca alkaloid vincamine, extracted from lesser periwinkle (Vinca minor) or Voacanga africana seeds. Grokipedia (AI-generated) describes it as developed by the Hungarian company Gedeon Richter and marketed in Hungary as Cavinton from 1978.
It has been used for more than three decades in several Asian and European countries for cerebrovascular disorders, though Wikipedia states that the evidence does not fully support a benefit in dementia or stroke. In the United States it is sold as a supplement despite the FDA regarding it as an unapproved new drug.
Its discussion in appearance-adjacent communities is as a general nootropic.

name: Sulbutiamine

angle.text: Sulbutiamine is prescribed for fatigue in France and sold elsewhere, with users taking it for energy, motivation and mental stamina. Human data are sparse and no appearance outcome has been studied.

summary: Lipid-soluble thiamine (B1) derivative prescribed for fatigue in France and sold elsewhere as a supplement; human data are sparse.
note: Not FDA-approved as a drug; Grokipedia reports it appears on a US Department of Defense prohibited supplement list.
currentQuick:
Sulbutiamine is a synthetic compound made of two thiamine (vitamin B1) units joined by a disulfide bond, designed to be fat-soluble so it enters the body and brain more readily than thiamine. Servier first marketed it in France in 1973 as Arcalion for asthenia (weakness).
It is also sold as a nootropic supplement. Human evidence is limited to small studies; Wikipedia reports a 2017 uncontrolled trial in multiple sclerosis fatigue and notes it is unclear whether it helps with drowsiness. Nothing documents an appearance use.
How it works: After absorption it is reduced to thiamine by thiols such as cysteine or glutathione. Rodent and cell studies show it raises thiamine phosphate levels, including in brain tissue.
Risks and caveats: Trials mostly report headache and stomach discomfort at high doses. Wikipedia says daily use can lead to tolerance and paradoxical drowsiness. Other reports include diarrhea, insomnia, constipation and vertigo.
deepLead:
Sulbutiamine (isobutyrylthiamine disulfide) is a synthetic, lipophilic derivative of thiamine in which two thiamine molecules are linked by a disulfide bridge. Servier marketed it in France from 1973 as Arcalion, and it is prescribed there for asthenia.
It is also sold as a dietary supplement, and some users take it as a nootropic. Evidence is limited, and a 1980s French review found the data did not support use in fatigue.

name: Pyritinol

angle.text: Pyritinol is approved in several European countries for dementia-related impairment and sold in the US as a nootropic for memory and focus. Evidence is dated and mixed, and it has no appearance angle tested.

summary: Vitamin B6 disulfide analog approved in several European countries for dementia-related impairment and sold as a US nootropic supplement; evidence is dated and mixed.
note: Rare severe reactions reported, including cholestatic hepatitis and pancreatitis; not FDA-recognized as a drug.
currentQuick:
Pyritinol is a semi-synthetic compound made by linking two vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) molecules with a disulfide bridge, produced by Merck in 1961. It is approved in several European countries for chronically impaired brain function in dementia syndromes and has been sold as a nootropic supplement in the US since the early 1990s.
Human trials are mostly old and small, with mixed results, and none addresses appearance.
How it works: Grokipedia (AI-generated) describes effects on brain glucose metabolism and cholinergic activity in animal and lab work. Wikipedia reports a half-life of about 2.5 hours.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are nausea and headache; mild skin allergy is rare. A 2004 survey of six case reports linked it to severe cholestatic hepatitis in patients on several drugs, and acute pancreatitis and a photoallergic eruption are also reported. Induced pemphigus has been reported in the dermatology literature.
deepLead:
Pyritinol, also called pyrithioxine or pyridoxine disulfide, is a semi-synthetic water-soluble analog of vitamin B6 first produced by Merck in 1961. From the 1970s it was sold as a prescription and over-the-counter drug in several countries, and since the early 1990s as a nootropic supplement in the United States.
In several European countries it is approved for symptomatic treatment of chronically impaired brain function in dementia syndromes and for sequelae of head trauma; in France it is also approved for rheumatoid arthritis.

name: Meclofenoxate (Centrophenoxine)

angle.text: Centrophenoxine is promoted as an anti-aging nootropic, a reputation built on 1970s elderly-memory studies and a mouse-lifespan claim. People tie that to looking younger, but no study has examined skin.

summary: DMAE ester nootropic with 1970s elderly-memory studies and a mouse-lifespan claim behind its "anti-aging" reputation; no studies of skin.
note: Not FDA-approved; prescription-only in places such as Germany and Japan; sold as a supplement in the US.
currentQuick:
Meclofenoxate (centrophenoxine) is an ester of dimethylaminoethanol (DMAE) and 4-chlorophenoxyacetic acid. It is sold as a prescription drug in Japan and some European countries, under names such as Lucidril, and as a supplement in the US.
Its "anti-aging" reputation rests on lipofuscin (age pigment) findings in the brain and a reported 26.5 percent lifespan increase in mice. A 1977 study reported improved memory-test performance in elderly patients. No studies have tested it on skin.
How it works: It is classed as a cholinergic nootropic; animal studies report changes in brain monoamines and protection in cerebral ischemia models.
Risks and caveats: Rare effects include insomnia, dizziness, restlessness, tremor, depression, nausea and headache, which Wikipedia says may reflect overdose. Brazil lists it as a controlled substance (2023) and it is not FDA-approved.
deepLead:
Meclofenoxate, also called centrophenoxine, is an ester of dimethylethanolamine (DMAE) and 4-chlorophenoxyacetic acid. It is sold as a prescription drug in Japan and some European countries including Germany, Hungary and Austria, and as a supplement elsewhere.
Published human research is mostly from the 1970s and 1980s and animal work. A claim of a 26.5 percent lifespan increase in mice and a 1977 elderly memory study are the basis of its "anti-aging" reputation.

name: Bromantane

angle.text: Bromantane is a Russian stimulant-anxiolytic that users take for motivation and lower social stress, and some claim it raises testosterone for physique gains. Human data are small and mostly Russian-language, and the physique claim is anecdotal.

summary: Russian adamantane stimulant-anxiolytic traded as a motivation nootropic; human data are small and mostly Russian-language.
note: Banned in sport by WADA; not FDA-approved; no appearance trials.
currentQuick:
Bromantane is a Russian-developed drug, sold there as Ladasten for neurasthenia (fatigue). It is described as a mild stimulant with anxiety-reducing effects.
In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed for motivation, stress and recovery, not as a direct appearance treatment. Most human evidence comes from Russian-language studies, and no trials address appearance outcomes.
How it works: Animal research reports that it increases the enzymes that make dopamine (tyrosine hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase) instead of mainly blocking dopamine reuptake. The precise mechanism is not settled.
Risks and caveats: Russian studies report few side effects (about 3% of patients in one large study). Long-term data in healthy users are lacking. It is prescription-only in Russia, unapproved by the FDA, and banned by WADA since 1997.
deepLead:
Bromantane (also spelled bromantan; Russian brand name Ladasten) is a synthetic adamantane derivative, chemically N-(4-bromophenyl)adamantan-2-amine, that is related to amantadine and memantine. It is described in the literature as an atypical stimulant and anxiolytic and as an "actoprotector", a term used in Russian pharmacology for synthetic adaptogens said to raise resistance to physical and psychological stress. 
Bromantane was developed in the Soviet Union at the Zakusov Institute of Pharmacology in Moscow and is a prescription drug in Russia for neurasthenia (asthenia). It is not approved by the US Food and Drug Administration, and it has been on the World Anti-Doping Agency's prohibited list since 1997.  In looksmaxxing and nootropic circles it is discussed as a supplement for motivation, mood, stress resilience and recovery rather than as a direct appearance treatment. 
Most published human data are from Russian-language journals. Animal studies report that it increases the activity of enzymes involved in dopamine synthesis.  Proponents' claims about testosterone, prolactin and sexual function that circulate in forums have not been tested in published human trials.

name: Phosphatidylserine

angle.text: Phosphatidylserine is sold for memory and in sports products for recovery from exercise stress, which lifters tie to training harder. Trials are mainly in cognition, with none for appearance.

summary: Membrane phospholipid sold as a memory and recovery supplement; trials are mainly in cognition, none for appearance.
note: FDA health claim is qualified as limited and preliminary; EFSA found no established cause and effect.
currentQuick:
Phosphatidylserine is a fat-like molecule found in every cell membrane and concentrated in the brain. Supplements, now usually soy-derived, are sold for memory and recovery.
Human trials have mostly looked at cognition in older adults, children and athletes. None examine appearance outcomes, so its looksmaxxing role rests on supplement marketing.
How it works: PS helps anchor signalling proteins in neuron membranes and tags dying cells for removal by immune cells. How oral supplements might affect brain function is not settled.
Risks and caveats: A 2002 safety report found a daily regimen safe in elderly people. Supplements are unregulated products, and the FDA's 2003 health claim carries a disclaimer that the evidence is limited.
deepLead:
Phosphatidylserine (PS) is a glycerophospholipid found in all cell membranes, most abundant in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane and enriched in the brain, where it makes up roughly 13 to 15 percent of cortical phospholipids.  It is also sold as an oral dietary supplement, usually derived from soy lecithin, marketed for memory and cognition, and in sports and recovery products for exercise stress. 
In 2003 the US FDA allowed a qualified health claim for PS and cognitive decline, noting the supporting research was limited and preliminary, while the European Food Safety Authority in 2010 concluded that cause and effect had not been established for several PS claims.  Clinical trials have studied PS in older adults, children with ADHD and athletes.  Its role in appearance is indirect: forum discussion presents it as a cortisol-lowering recovery supplement, a claim for which no appearance-focused studies exist.

name: Dimethylaminoethanol (DMAE)

angle.text: DMAE is an ingredient in skin-firming creams marketed for a tighter, smoother look, and is also sold as a nootropic. No human trial isolates its skin effect.

summary: Industrial amino alcohol used in skin-firming creams and sold as a nootropic; no human trial isolates its skin effect.
note: Concentrated DMAE is a corrosive industrial chemical; cosmetic claims lack published human trials in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
DMAE is mostly an industrial chemical used in plastics and resins. It also appears in some firming skin-care products and in oral nootropic supplements.
The sources reviewed report no human trial results for either use, so claims about skin tightening rest on marketing.
How it works: The way DMAE might affect skin or the brain is not established. Animal studies point to possible memory effects, while no mechanism for skin firming is documented.
Risks and caveats: The pure liquid is flammable and corrosive and carries hazard warnings. Safety data for cosmetic or supplement use in people are not summarised in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Dimethylaminoethanol (DMAE, also dimethylethanolamine, DMEA or deanol) is a colourless amino alcohol with the formula (CH3)2NCH2CH2OH. It is mainly an industrial chemical, used as a curing agent for polyurethanes and epoxy resins and as an intermediate for other compounds. 
It is also an ingredient in some skin-care products marketed for firming and improving skin tone, and its bitartrate salt is sold as an oral nootropic supplement.  Wikipedia reports no human trial results for either use, and animal work cited there concerns memory rather than skin.  Only one registered human study involving a DMAE-containing skin product was found, and it tested a multi-ingredient combination.

name: Methylsulfonylmethane (MSM)

chain: Sulfur supplied to skin and hair
angle.text: Users take MSM in the hope of softer, lighter skin, stronger hair and nails, and joints that stay comfortable for training. Forum posters also claim it lightens eye colour and preserves height through the day. A few small skin trials exist; the other claims rest on anecdote.

summary: Sulfur supplement sold for skin, hair and joints; a few small skin trials, but evidence is weak overall.
note: Eye- and skin-lightening claims come from anecdote only.
currentQuick:
MSM is a sulfur compound found in trace amounts in foods and sold as a supplement for joints, skin, hair and nails. It is cheap and widely available.
Small trials report improved wrinkles and hydration, but they are tiny and short. Claims about lightening skin or eye colour appear only in anecdotes.
How it works: How MSM acts in the body is poorly understood. It is related to DMSO and may have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects in lab studies. In topical products it may help other ingredients penetrate skin.
Risks and caveats: Animal studies suggest very low toxicity and it has a GRAS non-objection letter for a branded form. It has no approved medical uses. Human long-term data are limited.
deepLead:
Methylsulfonylmethane (MSM, dimethyl sulfone) is a small organic sulfur compound, (CH3)2SO2, that occurs naturally in trace amounts in some plants, foods and human blood. It is sold as a dietary supplement for joint comfort, skin, hair and nails, and it appears in topical products. 
The US FDA has not approved MSM for any medical use, though a manufacturer's 2007 notification that a branded form is generally recognised as safe (GRAS) received a non-objection letter in 2008.  Wikipedia describes the evidence for most claims as weak. Small randomised trials of skin and hair outcomes exist, while an osteoarthritis review reported no definitive evidence of superiority over placebo. 
On looksmax.org it is discussed for skin, hair texture and joint health, with claims about skin or eye lightening that appear in anecdote only.

name: Hydroxycitric acid (HCA)

chain: Blocks an enzyme in fat synthesis
angle.text: HCA from Garcinia cambogia is promoted as a fat blocker that users take to get leaner. The mechanism comes from lab enzyme data, and human trials have measured weight change rather than visible leanness, with small short-term differences reported.

summary: Garcinia-derived acid sold as a fat blocker; trials show at most a small short-term weight difference.
note: Gastrointestinal side effects and liver-injury reports with Garcinia products.
currentQuick:
HCA is the main acid in the rind of the Garcinia cambogia fruit and is sold as a fat-loss supplement, often in fat-burner blends.
Trials are mixed: a 1998 JAMA trial found no advantage over placebo, and a 2011 meta-analysis found a small short-term difference of uncertain relevance.
How it works: In the lab HCA inhibits ATP citrate lyase, an enzyme that supplies building blocks for fat synthesis. Whether this reduces body fat in people is what trials have tested.
Risks and caveats: A meta-analysis reported about twice the rate of gastrointestinal side effects. It is considered contraindicated in colitis or inflammatory bowel disease, and reviews of liver injury list Garcinia products.
deepLead:
Hydroxycitric acid (HCA) is a derivative of citric acid found in the fruit rinds of tropical plants, most notably Garcinia cambogia (Malabar tamarind, also called G. gummi-gutta), and in roselle (Hibiscus sabdariffa).  The (-)-isomer found in Garcinia is a competitive inhibitor of ATP citrate lyase, an enzyme that supplies acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis, which is the basis for its marketing as a fat-loss supplement. 
Human trials of Garcinia extract for weight loss have given mixed results. A 12-week randomised trial published in JAMA in 1998 reported no significant advantage over placebo, while a 2011 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials reported a small weight-loss difference of uncertain clinical relevance and more gastrointestinal adverse effects.  Reviews of liver injury cite Garcinia-containing products among implicated supplements, though HCA's specific role is unclear.

name: Hydroxycut

angle.text: Hydroxycut is a mass-market caffeine-based fat burner that people use during cutting phases to get leaner. Current formulas centre on caffeine and plant extracts such as robusta coffee. Evidence for the branded products specifically comes mostly from manufacturer-linked studies.

summary: Mass-market caffeine fat burner with a 2009 FDA warning and recall after liver-injury reports; independent efficacy trials are lacking.
note: FDA warned consumers in 2009 and the maker recalled products; liver injury case series exist.
currentQuick:
Hydroxycut is a mainstream fat-burner brand launched in 2002 by MuscleTech and now sold by Iovate. Its formulas have changed over time, from ephedra-era versions to current caffeine and coffee-extract blends.
The company cites two studies of its coffee extract, and critics have said independent evidence for the finished products is lacking.
How it works: Current products rely mainly on caffeine, a stimulant, and robusta coffee extract (chlorogenic acids), marketed as supporting metabolism and weight loss alongside diet and exercise.
Risks and caveats: In 2009 the FDA warned consumers to stop using Hydroxycut products after reports of liver damage and at least one death, and the maker recalled them. Case series describe liver injury, and stimulant versions carry caffeine warnings.
deepLead:
Hydroxycut is a brand of over-the-counter weight-loss and fat-burner dietary supplements introduced in 2002 and developed by MuscleTech, a Toronto-area company whose assets were largely sold in 2003-2004 to Iovate Health Sciences, which continues to sell it.  Formulations have changed repeatedly: early versions contained ephedra, later ones included ingredients associated with liver injury, and current products are built around caffeine and plant extracts such as robusta coffee extract. 
On 1 May 2009 the US FDA warned consumers to stop using Hydroxycut products after reports of serious health problems including liver damage and at least one death, and the manufacturer issued a voluntary recall; reformulated products were later returned to market.  Case series in the medical literature describe liver injury associated with Hydroxycut. 
The company markets the products for adults combining them with diet and exercise and cites two human studies of its primary ingredient, while critics have said published evidence of effectiveness and safety for the final products is lacking.

name: Dexatrim

angle.text: Dexatrim is a long-running diet-pill brand used as an appetite suppressant and energy aid for losing weight. Current versions are caffeine and green-tea blends. The brand's own products have little trial evidence for fat loss, though its ingredients are studied individually.

summary: A long-running diet-pill brand that dropped PPA after stroke concerns and now sells caffeine and green-tea blends with little trial evidence.
note: Original PPA formula was withdrawn after FDA action in 2000; case reports describe cardiac and neurological events.
currentQuick:
Dexatrim is an over-the-counter diet pill brand sold since the 1970s. It is marketed for appetite control and energy while dieting.
Its original ingredient, phenylpropanolamine, was removed after the FDA's 2000 action. Current versions use stimulant and botanical blends, and no trials of the branded products were found.
How it works: Earlier versions used a sympathomimetic amine that reduces appetite. Current versions rely on caffeine, green tea extract and other ingredients marketed to raise energy expenditure, though evidence for these ingredients is limited.
Risks and caveats: PPA-era use was linked in case reports and a Yale study to hemorrhagic stroke, heart injury and neurological effects. Current stimulant blends carry caffeine-type effects such as insomnia and palpitations, and labels advise caution with heart conditions and pregnancy.
deepLead:
Dexatrim is a brand of over-the-counter weight-loss products sold as appetite suppressants and energy aids. The line was introduced in the 1970s by Thompson Medical Company and originally relied on phenylpropanolamine (PPA), a sympathomimetic also used in cold remedies . After regulatory action in 2000 PPA was removed, and current capsules are multi-ingredient stimulant blends built around caffeine, green tea extract, ginseng and other botanicals .
PPA-era Dexatrim appears in the medical literature mainly through safety case reports, including a myocardial injury case in a young woman using the product at labelled amounts and a case of transient memory loss and aphasia . Researchers also published a pharmacokinetic study of the controlled-release caplet . No randomized trials of current Dexatrim formulations were found, and its individual ingredients have limited evidence for weight loss .

name: CortiSlim

angle.text: CortiSlim was marketed to people wanting to lose weight, especially around the midsection, by controlling cortisol. The idea that supplements can trim stress-related belly fat is a marketing theory; no published trials test the product, and its advertising drew an FTC action.

summary: A cortisol-themed diet supplement whose advertising drew an FTC false-advertising action and which has no published trials behind it.
note: Research claims in its advertising were found false by the FTC.
currentQuick:
CortiSlim is a brand of weight-loss supplements marketed around lowering the stress hormone cortisol. It combines herbal blends including magnolia bark, green tea and banana leaf extracts.
The FTC found its claims of supporting research to be false, and no independent clinical trials were found.
How it works: The marketing proposed that blends could modulate cortisol, appetite and blood sugar. No studies were found showing the product changes cortisol or body weight.
Risks and caveats: Ingredients include bitter orange (synephrine), green tea extract and vanadyl sulfate, whose safety profiles are discussed elsewhere in the literature. The product's marketing was the subject of FTC action and the original marketer went bankrupt.
deepLead:
CortiSlim is a branded dietary supplement line that was marketed as a "cortisol control" weight-loss formula. It was sold by CortiSlim International and earlier by Window Rock Enterprises, and it combined several herbal blends such as magnolia bark, green tea extract and banana leaf extract .
The product was marketed on the idea that stress-related cortisol promotes fat storage. The US Federal Trade Commission challenged advertising for cortisol-related weight-loss products, and Wikipedia reports that the marketer lost a false-advertising case and later went bankrupt; the line was acquired in 2008 . No independent clinical trials of the product were found.

name: Metabolife

angle.text: Metabolife 356 was the best-selling fat burner of its era, taken by people dieting for a leaner look. Its ephedra-caffeine combination has been studied for short-term weight loss. It is documented here mainly as a historical example after the federal ephedra ban.

summary: The best-selling ephedra fat burner of its era, ended by cardiovascular safety concerns, litigation, a federal ephedra ban and bankruptcy.
note: Ephedra supplements were banned in the US in 2004 after reports of heart attacks and strokes.
currentQuick:
Metabolife 356 was a top-selling stimulant diet supplement combining ephedra and caffeine, sold from the mid-1990s by Metabolife International.
After adverse-event reports, a congressional investigation and the 2004 FDA ephedra ban, the company went bankrupt in 2005.
How it works: Ephedra's alkaloids and caffeine stimulate the sympathetic nervous system, raising heart rate and metabolic rate and suppressing appetite.
Risks and caveats: A 2004 randomized trial found cardiovascular effects, and case reports describe heart attack, stroke, psychosis and diabetic ketoacidosis. Ephedra dietary supplements have been banned in the US since 2004.
deepLead:
Metabolife was a San Diego company founded in the 1990s by Michael Ellis, best known for Metabolife 356, an ephedra- and caffeine-based weight-loss and energy supplement sold largely through a customer-driven distribution model . At its peak it was the top-selling dietary weight-loss supplement in the United States .
Ephedra raises heart rate and blood pressure, and the product was the subject of adverse-event reports, a randomized trial that found cardiovascular effects, a congressional investigation, litigation and, in 2004, a US ban on ephedra-containing supplements . The company filed for bankruptcy in 2005 and its non-ephedra assets were later sold .

name: Chromium nicotinate

angle.text: Chromium nicotinate is taken for fat loss, muscle gain and blood sugar control, on the idea that chromium improves how the body handles carbohydrate. Trials of chromium forms have measured body composition directly, with mixed results.

summary: A niacin-bound chromium supplement sold for fat loss and glucose control; trials of chromium forms show no reliable body-composition benefit.
note: Most research covers chromium picolinate, not nicotinate; EFSA found weight claims unsupported.
currentQuick:
Chromium nicotinate is a form of the trace mineral chromium bound to niacin, sold in supplements marketed for weight loss, muscle building and blood sugar.
Reviews of chromium supplements report no reliable evidence for body-weight effects, and a trial of chromium nicotinate in type 2 diabetes found no benefit.
How it works: Chromium has been proposed to enhance insulin signaling, possibly through a chromium-binding peptide, but the active form is unknown and effects in living subjects have not been shown.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia reports little evidence of toxicity at typical amounts, with rare allergic reactions, headache, insomnia and kidney or liver reports (mostly picolinate). It may interact with medicines, including insulin.
deepLead:
Chromium nicotinate (chromium polynicotinate) is a form of trivalent chromium bound to niacin, sold as a dietary supplement alongside chromium picolinate and chromium chloride. Chromium products have been marketed for fat loss, muscle gain and blood sugar control .
Reviews cited by Wikipedia report no reliable evidence for body-weight effects: a 2013 Cochrane review found no reliable evidence on which to base firm decisions, and the European Food Safety Authority found evidence insufficient for body-weight claims . A randomized trial of chromium nicotinate in people with type 2 diabetes found no effect on insulin sensitivity, glycemic control or lipids . Most published work on chromium forms concerns picolinate rather than nicotinate.

name: Policosanol

angle.text: Policosanol is a sugarcane-wax supplement used for cholesterol, and it is listed on the wiki among metabolism-related products. Users who include it in fat-loss stacks do so through the general-health link. Lipid results are debated, and no studies address body fat or appearance.

summary: A sugarcane-wax alcohol mixture sold for cholesterol, with disputed lipid results and no evidence on body fat or looks.
note: Cuban trials were positive but non-Cuban replications were not; not studied for appearance.
currentQuick:
Policosanol is a mix of waxy alcohols from sugarcane, sold as a cholesterol supplement. It comes from Cuban research in the 1990s.
Cuban studies reported lower cholesterol, but later trials elsewhere did not replicate this, and it has not been studied for fat loss or appearance.
How it works: Cell studies suggest it may suppress cholesterol synthesis via AMP-kinase and effects on HMG-CoA reductase; human effects are disputed.
Risks and caveats: A 2005 meta-analysis described it as well tolerated, per Wikipedia. EFSA rejected a cholesterol claim in 2011, per Grokipedia.
deepLead:
Policosanol is a mixture of long-chain primary alcohols, chiefly octacosanol, extracted from plant waxes such as sugarcane wax and sold as a cholesterol-lowering dietary supplement . It was first developed commercially in Cuba . It is not an appearance compound; the wiki lists it among fat- and metabolism-related supplements.
Early Cuban trials reported lower cholesterol , but a randomized trial published in JAMA in 2006 examined policosanol in people with hypercholesterolemia , and Wikipedia notes that groups outside Cuba have not reproduced the Cuban results . A 2018 meta-analysis cited by Wikipedia reported improved lipid profiles , and the European Food Safety Authority rejected a cholesterol health claim in 2011, according to Grokipedia . No evidence was found of effects on body fat or appearance.

name: Red yeast rice

angle.text: Red yeast rice is taken for cholesterol and appears in longevity routines as part of keeping the body healthy over decades. Its cholesterol effect is studied; it is not used for a direct appearance outcome.

summary: Fermented rice containing natural lovastatin, studied for cholesterol; contents are inconsistent and it has no evidence for looks.
note: Monacolin content varies and some products carry citrinin; EFSA found no safe intake for monacolin preparations.
currentQuick:
Red yeast rice is rice fermented with Monascus mold, used for centuries in Chinese food and medicine and now sold for cholesterol.
Trials report lower LDL cholesterol, but it has not been studied for appearance or weight outcomes.
How it works: It contains monacolin K, identical to lovastatin, which inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that makes cholesterol.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects resemble statins, including muscle and liver problems. Monacolin content varies, some products contain citrinin, EFSA in 2018 found no safe intake, and the FDA treats products with substantial monacolin K as drugs.
deepLead:
Red yeast rice is rice fermented with the mold Monascus purpureus. It has long been used in Chinese cooking and traditional medicine and is now sold as a supplement for cholesterol . It contains monacolins, including monacolin K, which is chemically identical to the drug lovastatin .
Randomized trials report lower LDL cholesterol , and a large Chinese trial of the extract Xuezhikang in post-heart-attack patients reported fewer coronary events . Safety concerns include variable monacolin content, possible citrinin contamination and statin-like muscle and liver effects . It is included here as a longevity and cardiovascular supplement; no evidence on appearance outcomes was found.

name: Fucoidan

angle.text: Fucoidan is sold in longevity circles as a seaweed extract for healthy ageing and skin. Most findings come from cell and animal studies on inflammation and skin biology; human trials on appearance have not been run.

summary: A brown-seaweed sulfated sugar sold as a longevity supplement; lab results are plentiful, human appearance data absent.
note: Not approved as a drug anywhere; products vary widely in composition.
currentQuick:
Fucoidan is a family of sulfated polysaccharides extracted from brown seaweeds such as kombu and wakame. It is sold as a supplement and appears in longevity-focused product lines.
Cell and animal studies report anti-inflammatory, antiviral and antioxidant activity. Human trials are small and mostly address medical conditions; none found test a cosmetic or appearance outcome.
How it works: Its bioactivity is attributed to its fucose backbone and sulfate groups, which can bind proteins involved in inflammation, clotting and viral attachment in laboratory systems. Activity depends on the seaweed source, molecular weight and extraction method.
Risks and caveats: Evidence for human safety is described as limited and product quality varies. It shows anticoagulant activity in lab tests, and seaweed products can carry variable iodine and metal content. It is not approved as a drug in any country.
deepLead:
Fucoidan is a group of sulfated polysaccharides, built largely from the sugar fucose, found in the cell walls of brown seaweeds and in a few marine invertebrates such as sea cucumbers and sea urchins. Commercial material is usually extracted from species including Fucus vesiculosus, Laminaria japonica (kombu), Undaria pinnatifida (wakame) and Cladosiphon okamuranus. Its structure varies with species, season and extraction method, which makes products hard to compare.
It is sold as a dietary supplement, food additive and cosmetic ingredient, and appears in the longevity-supplement category as a general-purpose marine extract. Laboratory work has reported anti-inflammatory, anticoagulant, antiviral, antioxidant and antitumour activity in cells and animals.
Wikipedia states that, as of its 2019-era sources, the evidence consisted of laboratory studies, early-stage trials and case reports, that no advanced clinical trials had been reported, and that no national regulator had designated it safe for human use. No published study found in these sources tests fucoidan for facial appearance, skin ageing or any other cosmetic outcome.
